what: Polling means the client keeps asking the server whether something changed. Short polling asks on a timer; long polling holds each request open until there is news or a timeout, then asks again.
like: Like asking 'are we there yet?' every few minutes (short), versus asking once and the driver only answers when you arrive (long).
why: The simplest way to get near-live data, with no special server support for short polling
Works everywhere, through any proxy, and is easy to debug
A good fit for job status, deploy progress and slow-changing dashboards

steps.d: Short polling calls the endpoint every N seconds. Pick N from how stale the data may be, not from what feels fast.
Return ETag and answer 304 Not Modified when nothing changed, so the response has no body.
Long polling: the server waits until an event or a timeout, replies, and the client immediately asks again. Latency drops, but each client holds a connection.
Stop when the job is done. Back off the interval when nothing changes, and add jitter so clients do not all poll at the same instant.
Pause when the tab is hidden (Page Visibility API) and refresh immediately when it returns.

numbers.l: the long-poll timeout RFC 6202 calls the safer choice (experiments worked up to 120 s)
default browser timeout for a pending request, though many network devices time out sooner
how often Chrome runs chained timers on pages hidden for over 5 minutes (intensive throttling)

choices.d: Short polling is simplest and wasteful. Long polling gives near-instant updates with fewer empty responses, but holds a connection per client and needs server support.
Every poll costs a request and battery. Use ETag/304 to keep empty polls tiny, grow the interval while nothing changes, and stop when done.
Schedule the next poll after the previous one finishes, otherwise a slow response lets requests pile up.
If you poll faster than every few seconds or many clients poll the same data, move to SSE or WebSocket.

instead.why: Server pushes updates over one stream, with no repeated requests
When the client also sends often and latency matters

breaks.d: A fixed interval fires again before the slow response has returned.
breaks.fix: Schedule the next poll after the previous completes, and abort the old one

breaks.d: Many clients poll on aligned schedules, for example right after a deploy.
breaks.fix: Add random jitter and back off when nothing changes

breaks.d: Background tabs still send requests, or timers get throttled and run late.
breaks.see: Wasted battery and data, bursts when you return
breaks.fix: Pause on visibilitychange and refetch once when visible

say: For job status I poll with a chained timeout, ETag so empty polls are 304, and I stop as soon as the job reaches a final state.
I pause polling when the tab is hidden and refresh on return, and I add jitter so clients do not poll in lockstep.
If I need sub-second updates or many clients watch the same data, I move to SSE or WebSocket instead of polling harder.

followups.q: Why use setTimeout instead of setInterval?
followups.a: setInterval fires on a fixed clock, so a slow response lets requests overlap. A timeout scheduled after the response keeps exactly one poll in flight.

followups.q: What is the catch with long polling?
followups.a: Each client holds an open request, so servers and proxies need enough capacity, and timeouts must be shorter than any proxy in between, for example about 30 s.

followups.q: How do you make polling cheap?
followups.a: Conditional requests: send If-None-Match and let the server return 304 with no body when nothing changed.

today: Polling is still the simplest correct choice for status checks and slow dashboards. Server-state libraries such as TanStack Query provide refetchInterval for it, and the Page Visibility API lets you pause when nobody is looking.

check.q: A long-poll timeout of about what is the safer choice per RFC 6202?
check.why: Many network devices time out early, so 30 s is safer than the browser default of 300 s.

check.q: Your poll takes 6 s but the interval is 5 s. What goes wrong and what fixes it?
check.a: Requests overlap; schedule the next poll after the response
check.why: Chained timeouts keep one request in flight.

check.q: What response makes an unchanged poll cheap?
check.why: A conditional request returns no body when nothing changed.
